Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : BM3728 : Environmental Biotechnology Laboratory { 0-0-3 / 2}

Subject Nature : Practical

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Water analysis: Determination of pH, electrical conductivity, alkalinity, Hardness, total suspended solids (TSS) and total dissolved solids (TDS) in water samples.
Wastewater analysis: Determination of dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand, chemical oxygen demand in wastewater samples.
Soil analysis: Determination of organic matter, cation exchange capacity and acidity in soil samples.
Microorganisms for bioremediation: Isolation and molecular identification of bacteria for bioremediation, Characterization of microorganisms
Tolerance study: Determination of maximum tolerable concentration for given sample of bacteria
Biodegradation studies for the removal of toxic pollutants, Biosorption studies for the removal of heavy metals and dyes.
Bioleaching studies for the recovery of heavy metals and dyes.

Course Objective

1 .

To provide hands-on experience in analyzing environmental samples
2 .

To equip students with practical knowledge of microbial techniques for isolating and characterizing environmental microflora.
3 .

To introduce methods for assessing and mitigating environmental pollution through biodegradation, biosorption, and bioleaching techniques.
4 .

To foster an understanding of the relationship between biological systems and environmental sustainability

Course Outcome

1 .

Upon successful completion of the laboratory course, students will be able to:
1. Perform accurate measurements of physical, chemical, and biological parameters in water, wastewater and soil samples.
2. Detect and quantify pollutants such as heavy metals, dyes, carbon monoxide, and oxides of sulfur and nitrogen in various media.
3. Isolate and identify microflora (bacteria, fungi, mold, and pollen) from diverse environmental samples using standard microbiological techniques.
4. Conduct biodegradation studies for organic pollutants and biosorption experiments for heavy metal and dye removal.
5. Integrate biotechnological approaches to support environmental conservation and sustainable development.

Essential Reading

1 .

Pepper, Ian L., Charles P. Gerba, and Jeffrey W. Brendecke, Environmental microbiology: a laboratory manual., Academic Press , 1995

Course Details

Subject {L-T-P / C} : CE4400 : Hydraulic Engineering { 3-0-0 / 3}

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Basic properties of water Determination of hydrostatic forces Kinematics of flow Potential flow Continuity, Energy and Momentum principles. [8 hrs]
Module II: Open Channel Flow: Channel Characteristics and parameters, Uniform, flow, Critical flow, Specific Energy concepts, Gradually Varied Flows, Rapidly Varied flow with special reference to hydraulic jump. [10 hrs]
Module III: Boundary Layer Theory, Boundary layer characteristics, Integral, Momentum equation, onset of turbulence, properties of turbulent flow, skin friction, drag, lift and circulation. [8 hrs]
Module IV: Pipe Flow: Laminar and Turbulent, flow in Smooth and Rough pipes, pipe network analysis, Losses in pipes. [10 hrs]

Course Objective

1 .

1. To gain advanced knowledge on fluid statics and fluid dynamics mainly applicable to Civil Engineering
2 .

2. To apply the knowledge of fluid mechanics to water application
3 .

3. To gain knowledge of Water mechanics which is mainly on channel flow and pipe flow

Course Outcome

1 .

After the completion of this course, students will be able to:
CO1: Understand the basic concepts of fluid statics, kinematics and fluid dynamics.
CO2: Ability to explain the terms of the open channel flow equations and explain the
interactions among the terms.
CO3: Ability to explain the physical mechanisms of hydraulic jumps, surges, and critical,
uniform and gradually varying flows.
CO4: To understand the concept of boundary layer theory and its applications.
CO5: To understand and analyse the pipe flow and losses in the pipe.

Subject Nature : Theory

Syllabus

Module 1 :

Module I: Review of grammar and basic writing: Basic grammar, punctuation, apostrophe, structure of critical sentences.
Module II: Syntax and Semantics: Evaluation of sentence structure, complex phrasing, separation of structure and meaning, deep and surface structures, error analysis
Module III: Indexing, Abstracting and Note Taking: Composition to meaning meaning to composition, key word analysis, phrasing thoughts and composition.

Module V: Editing and Formatting: Grammatical particles, structure, colloquial expressions, native voices and nuances, standard phrasing, academic formatting, style, native speakers’ style.

Course Objective

Introduce the students to the universe of scientific and technical writing.
2 .

Enhance the technical writing skills for clear and unbiased articulation of ideas. Enhance the technical writing skills for clear and unbiased articulation of ideas.
3 .

Enable the students to evaluate research papers and academic theses critically.
4 .

Introduce multiple genres of writing for effective academic communication.

Course Outcome

1 .

CO1: Introduce the universe of scientific and critical writing to PhD students so that they can write research papers and their own theses.
CO2: Help students understand how critical research is documented with a special focus on language, writing, and editing.
CO3: Allow students to analyze academic writing critically and address issues of their own writing.
CO4: Enable students to make appropriate grammatical and lexical choices that will improve the quality of research writing.
